Vorticity blowup in 2D compressible Euler equations

Jiajie Chen Address: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University, New York, NY 10012. Email address: jiajie.chen@cims.nyu.edu , Giorgio Cialdea Address: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University, New York, NY 10012. Email address: giorgio.cialdea@cims.nyu.edu , Steve Shkoller Address: Department of Mathematics, University of California Davis, Davis, CA 95616. Email address: shkoller@math.ucdavis.edu and Vlad Vicol Address: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University, New York, NY 10012. Email address: vicol@cims.nyu.edu
Abstract.

We prove finite-time vorticity blowup for smooth solutions of the 2D compressible Euler equations with smooth, localized, and non-vacuous initial data. The vorticity blowup occurs at the time of the first singularity, and is accompanied by an axisymmetric implosion in which the swirl velocity enjoys full stability, as opposed to finite co-dimension stability.

1. Introduction

We consider the isentropic compressible Euler equations in multiple space dimensions

(1.1a) ∂t(ρ​𝐮)+div⁡(ρ​𝐮⊗𝐮)+∇p\displaystyle\partial_{t}(\rho\mathbf{u})+\operatorname{div}(\rho\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u})+\nabla p =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
(1.1b) ∂tρ+div⁡(ρ​𝐮)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho\mathbf{u}) =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
where 𝐮:ℝd×[0,∞)→ℝd\mathbf{u}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is the velocity vector field and ρ:ℝd×[0,∞)→ℝ+\rho\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is the strictly positive density function. The pressure p:ℝd×[0,∞)→ℝ+p\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is determined from the density via the ideal gas law
(1.1c) p=1γ​ργ,p=\tfrac{1}{\gamma}\rho^{\gamma},
where γ>1\gamma>1 is the adiabatic exponent. We supplement the Euler equations with initial data
(1.1d) (𝐮,ρ)|t=0=(𝐮0,ρ0),(\mathbf{u},\rho)|_{t=0}=(\mathbf{u}_{0},\rho_{0}),

which is as nice as it gets. By this, we mean that (𝐮0,ρ0)∈C∞​(ℝd)(\mathbf{u}_{0},\rho_{0})\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), ρ0≥constant>0\rho_{0}\geq{\rm constant}>0 on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and (|𝐮0​(x)|,ρ0​(x))→(0,constant)(|\mathbf{u}_{0}(x)|,\rho_{0}(x))\to(0,{\rm constant}) as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, at a sufficiently fast rate; here, d≥2d\geq 2 is the space dimension.

With these assumptions on (𝐮0,ρ0)(\mathbf{u}_{0},\rho_{0}), the classical well-posedness theory [39, 52, 50] guarantees the existence of a maximal time T>0T>0, and of a unique solution (𝐮,ρ)∈C∞​(ℝd×(0,T))(\mathbf{u},\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,T)) of the Cauchy problem for the Euler equations (1.1). Generically, we expect that T<∞T<\infty, a singularity forms in finite time [53, 49, 67].

While it is well-known that at the time TT of the first singularity the solution must develop infinite gradients, i.e. lim supt↗T‖(∇𝐮,∇ρ)​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(ℝd)=∞\limsup_{t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T}\|(\nabla\mathbf{u},\nabla\rho)(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=\infty, a complete classification of all possible singularity mechanisms attainable by smooth Euler solutions (𝐮,ρ)​(⋅,t)(\mathbf{u},\rho)(\cdot,t) as t↗T<∞t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T<\infty remains, to date, elusive.

For instance, while it is known that a pre-shock singularity [27, 29, 8, 6, 9, 10, 55, 56] or an implosion singularity [62, 63, 11, 5] may form as t↗Tt\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T from smooth initial conditions, it is an outstanding open problem to determine whether lim supt↗T‖ω⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(ℝd)=∞\limsup_{t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T}\|\omega(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=\infty, where ω=∇×𝐮\omega=\nabla\times\mathbf{u} denotes the fluid vorticity.

In the case that the Euler solution evolves to a stable gradient blowup at a time T<∞T<\infty, from generic, compressive, and smooth initial data, the vorticity ω⁡(⋅,t)\omega(\cdot,t) remains uniformly bounded in C1/3​(ℝd)C^{1/3}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], as was shown in [8, 6, 9, 10, 66]. The fact that the vorticity does not blow up at the time of the first gradient singularity11 1 The spacetime point at which the first gradient singularity forms is the point on the spacetime co-dimension-22 manifold of pre-shocks, with a minimal time coordinate (see [66]). should not come as a surprise for d=2d=2, since the specific vorticity ω/ρ\omega/\rho is transported by the fluid velocity:

(1.2) ∂t(ωρ)+(𝐮⋅∇)(ωρ)=0.\partial_{t}\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{\rho}\Bigr)+(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{\rho}\Bigr)=0\,.

Since the density in [8, 6, 9, 10, 66] remains bounded at the time of the first gradient blowup, and the initial datum is non-vacuous, it follows from the maximum principle for (1.2) that ‖ω⁡(⋅,T)‖L∞​(ℝ2)<∞\|\omega(\cdot,T)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}<\infty. For d=3d=3, the proof of this upper bound for the maximum vorticity is more subtle (see [10]).

The specific vorticity transport equation (1.2) shows that for d=2d=2 the vorticity can blow up at time TT only if an implosion singularity simultaneously develops at time TT, i.e. limt↗T‖ρ⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(ℝ2)\lim_{t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T}\|\rho(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}. This, however, need not be an if and only if statement. Indeed, the smooth implosions established in [62, 63, 5] are confined to radially symmetric solutions, and hence ω⁡(⋅,t)≡0\omega(\cdot,t)\equiv 0 for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. The only rigorous proof of a non-radially symmetric implosion from smooth initial data was recently established in [11] for d=3d=3. Such non-radial imploding solutions possess non-trivial vorticity, but establishing vorticity blowup is incongruous with the finite co-dimension stability framework employed in [11]. In particular, since vorticity waves propagate along fluid-velocity characteristics22 2 The specific vorticity ω/ρ\omega/\rho is transported when d=2d=2 (see (1.2)) and is Lie-advected when d=3d=3 (see (2.9))., there exists a distinguished initial fluid particle x∗x_{*} such that ω0​(x∗)\omega_{0}(x_{*}) is “carried to” the implosion along the fluid-velocity characteristics, thereby determining the vorticity ω⁡(⋅,T)\omega(\cdot,T) at the point of the implosion. As the stability analysis in [11] requires ω0\omega_{0} to be a finite co-dimension perturbation of the zero function, and does not specify the precise subspace associated to this finite co-dimension, it is not possible to guarantee that ω0​(x∗)≠0\omega_{0}(x_{*})\neq 0 (which must be ensured in order to establish vorticity blowup). We shall explain this issue in greater detail in Section 2.7 below.

The goal of this paper is to give the first proof of finite-time blowup for the vorticity in the compressible Euler equations, with smooth initial data — see Theorem 1.1 below.

1.1. The two-dimensional axisymmetric ansatz

In order to state our main result, it is convenient to first introduce a symmetric form of the isentropic Euler system (1.1), in which the fundamental variables are the fluid velocity 𝐮\mathbf{u} and the rescaled sound speed σ\sigma, which is defined by

σ=1α​d​pd​ρ=1α​ρα,α=γ−12.\sigma=\tfrac{1}{\alpha}\sqrt{\tfrac{dp}{d\rho}}=\tfrac{1}{\alpha}\rho^{\alpha},\quad\alpha=\tfrac{\gamma-1}{2}.

In terms of the unknowns 𝐮\mathbf{u} and σ\sigma the Euler equations (1.1) are equivalent to the following system33 3 In the full Euler system the specific entropy is transported along the flow of the vector field (∂t+𝐮⋅∇)(\partial_{t}+\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla). As such, for isentropic initial data (i.e., with constant specific entropy at time t=0t=0) the solution will remain isentropic up to the time TT of the very first singularity, which justifies the usage of the (1.1) and hence of (1.3) on [0,T][0,T].:

(1.3a) ∂t𝐮+𝐮⋅∇𝐮+ασ∇σ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}+\alpha\,\sigma\,\nabla\sigma =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
(1.3b) ∂tσ+𝐮⋅∇σ+α​σ​div​𝐮\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma+\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\sigma+\alpha\,\sigma\,\mathrm{div}\mathbf{u} =0.\displaystyle=0\,.

For the remainder of the paper, we restrict our analysis to the two-dimensional case: d=2d=2. As such, it is convenient to rewrite (1.3) in polar coordinates (R,θ)(R,\theta), defined as

R=|x|,θ=arctan⁡(x2x1),𝐞R=(cos⁡θ,sin ​θ),𝐞θ=(−sin ​θ,cos⁡θ).R=|x|,\quad\theta=\arctan\bigl(\tfrac{x_{2}}{x_{1}}\bigr),\quad\mathbf{e}_{R}=(\cos\theta,\text{sin }\theta),\quad\mathbf{e}_{\theta}=(-\text{sin }\theta,\cos\theta).

Throughout the paper, we shall use boldface font 𝐮,𝐔,…\mathbf{u},\mathbf{U},\ldots to denote vectors, and standard unbolded font u,U,…u,U,\ldots to denote scalars.

We analyze vorticity blowup within the class of two-dimensional axisymmetric flows, a class of flows with built-in rotation. That is, we consider a velocity field 𝐮\mathbf{u} with the following axisymmetry44 4 If uθ≡0u^{\theta}\equiv 0 in (1.4), we recover radially symmetric functions (𝐮,σ)(\mathbf{u},\sigma).:

(1.4) 𝐮=𝐮⁡(R,θ,t)=𝐮R+𝐮θ,𝐮R=uR​(R,t)​𝐞R,𝐮θ=uθ​(R,t)​𝐞θ,σ=σ⁡(R,t).\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}(R,\theta,t)=\mathbf{u}^{R}+\mathbf{u}^{\theta},\quad\mathbf{u}^{R}=u^{R}(R,t)\mathbf{e}_{R},\quad\mathbf{u}^{\theta}=u^{\theta}(R,t)\mathbf{e}_{\theta},\quad\sigma=\sigma(R,t).

The vorticity and velocity-divergence associated to the axisymmetric ansatz (1.4) are given by

ω\displaystyle\omega =ω(R,t)=(1R+∂R)uθ(R,t),\displaystyle=\omega(R,t)=\bigl(\tfrac{1}{R}+\partial_{R}\bigr)u^{\theta}(R,t),
div⁡𝐮\displaystyle\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u} =div𝐮R(R,t)=(1R+∂R)uR(R,t).\displaystyle=\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u}^{R}(R,t)=\bigl(\tfrac{1}{R}+\partial_{R}\bigr)u^{R}(R,t).

In general, for a smooth function f=f⁡(|x|):ℝ2→ℝf=f(|x|)\colon\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} we have div⁡(f​𝐞R)=R−1​∂R(R​f​(R))\operatorname{div}(f\mathbf{e}_{R})=R^{-1}\partial_{R}(Rf(R)); as such, we shall often abuse notation and simply write div⁡(f⁡(R))=R−1​∂R(R​f​(R))\operatorname{div}(f(R))=R^{-1}\partial_{R}(Rf(R)) in place of div⁡(f​𝐞R)\operatorname{div}(f\mathbf{e}_{R}).

In order to show that the two-dimensional axisymmetric ansatz (1.4) is preserved by the Euler evolution, we note that the system (1.3) is equivalent (for smooth solutions) to the system (1.7) below, which provides evolution equations for (uR,uθ,σ)=(uR,uθ,σ)​(R,t)(u^{R},u^{\theta},\sigma)=(u^{R},u^{\theta},\sigma)(R,t). For this purpose, it is convenient to recall the following identities, which hold for smooth functions f=f⁡(R)f=f(R):

(1.5) 𝐮R⋅∇f=uR​∂Rf,uθ​𝐞θ⋅∇(f​𝐞R)=1R​uθ​f​𝐞θ,uθ​𝐞θ⋅∇(f​𝐞θ)=−1R​uθ​f​𝐞R.\mathbf{u}^{R}\cdot\nabla f=u^{R}\partial_{R}f,\quad u^{\theta}\mathbf{e}_{\theta}\cdot\nabla(f\mathbf{e}_{R})=\tfrac{1}{R}u^{\theta}f\mathbf{e}_{\theta},\quad u^{\theta}\mathbf{e}_{\theta}\cdot\nabla(f\mathbf{e}_{\theta})=-\tfrac{1}{R}u^{\theta}f\mathbf{e}_{R}.

Using the ansatz (1.4) and the identities in (1.5), we may decompose the system (1.3) into radial and angular parts, leading to the equivalent formulation

(1.6a) ∂t𝐮R+𝐮R⋅∇𝐮R+𝐮θ⋅∇𝐮θ+ασ∇σ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}^{R}+\mathbf{u}^{R}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}^{R}+\mathbf{u}^{\theta}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}^{\theta}+\alpha\,\sigma\,\nabla\sigma =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
(1.6b) ∂t𝐮θ+𝐮R⋅∇𝐮θ+𝐮θ⋅∇𝐮R\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}^{\theta}+\mathbf{u}^{R}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}^{\theta}+\mathbf{u}^{\theta}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}^{R} =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
(1.6c) ∂tσ+𝐮R⋅∇σ+α​σ​div⁡𝐮R\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma+\mathbf{u}^{R}\cdot\nabla\sigma+\alpha\,\sigma\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u}^{R} =0.\displaystyle=0\,.

In terms of the scalar quantities (uR,uθ,σ)=(𝐮R⋅𝐞R,𝐮θ⋅𝐞θ,σ)(u^{R},u^{\theta},\sigma)=(\mathbf{u}^{R}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{R},\mathbf{u}^{\theta}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\theta},\sigma), the system (1.6) may be written as

(1.7a) ∂tuR+uR​∂RuR+α​σ​∂Rσ\displaystyle\partial_{t}u^{R}+u^{R}\partial_{R}u^{R}+\alpha\sigma\partial_{R}\sigma =1R​(uθ)2,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{R}(u_{\theta})^{2}\,,
(1.7b) ∂tuθ+uR​∂Ruθ+1R​uθ​uR\displaystyle\partial_{t}u^{\theta}+u^{R}\partial_{R}u^{\theta}+\tfrac{1}{R}u^{\theta}u^{R} =0,\displaystyle=0\,,
(1.7c) ∂tσ+uR​∂Rσ+α​σ​div⁡(uR)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma+u^{R}\partial_{R}\sigma+\alpha\,\sigma\operatorname{div}(u^{R}) =0.\displaystyle=0\,.

Both reformulations of the isentropic Euler system for two-dimensional axisymmetric flows, i.e. systems (1.6) and (1.7), when transformed to self-similar variables and coordinates (see (2.1) below), play important roles in the subsequent analysis. The self-similar version of (1.7) is used to study blowup profiles, while the self-similar version of (1.6) is used for energy estimates and the majority of bounds on the solution.

1.2. The main result

As mentioned in the discussion following (1.2), in two space dimensions the vorticity can blow up at time TT only if an implosion singularity simultaneously develops at time TT. Since we seek smooth Euler solutions on [0,T)[0,T), we aim to construct a stable perturbation (for the angular velocity) of a smoothly imploding self-similar solution, as was recently constructed in [62], and further refined in [5].

The self-similarity employed in [62], [5], and herein, is of the second kind. A similarity exponent r>1r>1 is determined as the solution of a nonlinear eigenvalue problem, and is then used to define the self-similar space ξ=R(T−t)1/r\xi=\frac{R}{(T-t)^{1/r}} and time s=−1r​log⁡(T−t)s=-\frac{1}{r}\log(T-t) coordinates, together with self-similar state variables (U,A,Σ)​(ξ,s)=r​(T−t)(r−1)/r​(uR,uθ,σ)​(R,t)(U,A,\Sigma)(\xi,s)=r(T-t)^{(r-1)/r}(u^{R},u^{\theta},\sigma)(R,t); see (2.1) below. The self-similar variables (U,A,Σ)(U,A,\Sigma) solve the self-similar version of the Euler system; see (2.3) below. Of particular interest for our analysis are special C∞C^{\infty}-smooth stationary solutions (U¯,0,Σ¯)(\bar{U},0,\bar{\Sigma}) to this self-similar system; we refer to the triplet (U¯,0,Σ¯)(\bar{U},0,\bar{\Sigma}) as the self-similar blowup profile.

We choose to work directly with the smooth imploding self-similar profiles (U¯,0,Σ¯)(\bar{U},0,\bar{\Sigma}) from [62, Theorem 1.2, Corollary 1.3], as these profiles, together with their repulsive properties (see (2.4b) below), are readily available for d=2d=2.55 5 While it is expected that the arguments in [5] also apply to the case that d=2d=2 (used in this paper), [5] only considers d=3d=3. The slight drawback of using the results from [62] is that we need to exclude an exceptional countable sequence of adiabatic exponents Γ={γn}n≥1\Gamma=\{\gamma_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}, which is possibly empty, and whose accumulation points can only be {1,2,∞}\{1,2,\infty\}. For each γ∉Γ\gamma\not\in\Gamma, it is shown in [62] (and recalled in Theorem 2.1 below) that there exists a discrete sequence of admissible blowup speeds {rk}k≥1⊂(1,r𝖾𝗒𝖾​(α))\{r_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}\subset(1,r_{\mathsf{eye}}(\alpha)), accumulating at the value r𝖾𝗒𝖾​(α)r_{\mathsf{eye}}(\alpha) defined in (2.2), such that the Euler equations (1.7) exhibit smooth, radially symmetric (meaning that uθ,A≡0u^{\theta},A\equiv 0), globally self-similar, imploding solutions with similarity exponent rkr_{k} and profile (U¯,0,Σ¯)(\bar{U},0,\bar{\Sigma}) (see Section 2.1 below). With this notation fixed, we state our main result.

Theorem 1.1 (Main result).

Fix a non-exceptional adiabatic exponent γ∉Γ\gamma\not\in\Gamma, let α=(γ−1)/2\alpha=(\gamma-1)/2, and let r>1r>1 be an admissible blowup speed satisfying (2.2), as in [62]. Then, there exists initial data (u0R,u0θ)∈Cc∞​(ℝ2)(u_{0}^{R},u_{0}^{\theta})\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) and σ0∈C∞​(ℝ2)\sigma_{0}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with σ0≥constant>0\sigma_{0}\geq{\rm constant}>0,66 6 The initial sound speed σ0\sigma_{0} may be chosen to equal a constant outside a compact set in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}; see Section 4. such that the solution (uR,uθ,σ)(u^{R},u^{\theta},\sigma) of (1.7) exhibits a finite time singularity at a time T<∞T<\infty. The radial velocity uRu^{R}, the sound speed σ\sigma, and the vorticity ω\omega all blow up at time TT. The blowup is asymptotically self-similar in the sense that

(1.8a) limt↗Tr​(T−t)r−1r​uR​((T−t)1r​ξ,t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T}r\big(T-t\big)^{\!\!{\frac{r-1}{r}}}u^{R}((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}\xi,t) =U¯​(ξ),\displaystyle=\bar{U}(\xi),
(1.8b) limt↗Tr​(T−t)r−1r​uθ​((T−t)1r​ξ,t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T}r\big(T-t\big)^{\!\!{\frac{r-1}{r}}}u^{\theta}((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}\xi,t) =0,\displaystyle=0,
(1.8c) limt↗Tr​(T−t)r−1r​σ​((T−t)1r​ξ,t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T}r\big(T-t\big)^{\!\!{\frac{r-1}{r}}}\sigma((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}\xi,t) =Σ¯​(ξ),\displaystyle=\bar{\Sigma}(\xi),
for ξ∈(0,∞)\xi\in(0,\infty), where U¯\bar{U} and Σ¯\bar{\Sigma} are the similarity profiles from [62]. The vorticity blows up at R=0R=0 as
(1.8d) limt↗T(T−t)r−1α​r​ω​(0,t)=ω0​(0)​(Σ¯​(0)r​σ0​(0))1α≠0,\lim_{t\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T}\big(T-t\big)^{\!\!{\frac{r-1}{\alpha r}}}\omega(0,t)=\omega_{0}(0)\left(\tfrac{\bar{\Sigma}(0)}{r\sigma_{0}(0)}\right)^{\!\!\frac{1}{\alpha}}\neq 0,

and there are no singularities away from the point of implosion: (R,t)=(0,T)(R,t)=(0,T).

An outline of the proof of Theorem 1.1 is given in Section 2. Before turning to the proof, we make a few comments concerning the statement of Theorem 1.1.

Remark 1.2 (The set of initial data for vorticity blowup).

As explained in Remark 4.2 below, there exists an open set X2X_{2} (a ball in a weighted Sobolev space) and a finite co-dimension set X1X_{1} such that the initial data in Theorem 1.1 may be taken such that (𝐮0R,σ0)∈X1(\mathbf{u}^{R}_{0},\sigma_{0})\in X_{1} and 𝐮0θ∈X2\mathbf{u}_{0}^{\theta}\in X_{2}. It is the fact that 𝐮0θ\mathbf{u}_{0}^{\theta} belongs to an open set which allows us to ensure that the initial vorticity ω0\omega_{0} does not vanish at R=0R=0.

Remark 1.3 (The curl blows up slower than the divergence).

Since ω0​(0)≠0\omega_{0}(0)\neq 0, identity (1.8d) shows that the vorticity blows up at R=0R=0 at the rate (T−t)−r−1α​r(T-t)^{-\frac{r-1}{\alpha r}}. Moreover, since the admissible blowup speed rr satisfies the constraint (2.2), it follows that 0<r−1α​r<r𝖾𝗒𝖾​(α)−1α​r𝖾𝗒𝖾​(α)<10<\frac{r-1}{\alpha\,r}<\frac{r_{\mathsf{eye}}(\alpha)-1}{\alpha\,r_{\mathsf{eye}}(\alpha)}<1 for all α>0\alpha>0, and therefore ∫0T‖ω⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​𝑑t≈∫0T|ω⁡(0,t)|​𝑑t<+∞\int_{0}^{T}\|\omega(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt\approx\int_{0}^{T}|\omega(0,t)|dt<+\infty. As the magnitude of vorticity is integrable in time, there does not exist a Beale-Kato-Majda type blowup criterium for the compressible Euler equations. As to the effects of compression, from (1.8a) and (2.4e), we have that |div⁡𝐮⁡(0,t)|≈(T−t)−1​(2/r)​|U¯′​(0)|=(T−t)−1​(r−1)/(α​r)|\!\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u}(0,t)|\approx(T-t)^{-1}(2/r)|\bar{U}^{\prime}(0)|=(T-t)^{-1}(r-1)/(\alpha r), which implies that ∫0T‖div⁡𝐮⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​𝑑t=+∞\int_{0}^{T}\|\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt=+\infty. The fact that div⁡u\operatorname{div}u blows up faster than ω\omega indicates that sound waves steepen in compression much faster than particles can “swirl”.

Remark 1.4 (There are no singularities away from R=0R=0 and t=Tt=T).

While Theorem 1.1 shows that the rescaled sound speed σ⁡(0,t)\sigma(0,t) and the magnitude of the gradients |∇𝐮|​(0,t)|\nabla\mathbf{u}|(0,t) and |∇σ|​(0,t)|\nabla\sigma|(0,t) blow up as t↗Tt\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T, we emphasize that, by construction, the Euler solution in Theorem 1.1 does not form singularities for times t<Tt<T, and moreover, as t↗Tt\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T no singularities develop at points x∈ℝ2x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} with x≠0x\neq 0. Indeed, for x≠0x\neq 0 and t∈[0,T)t\in[0,T) arbitrary, upper bounds for |𝐮⁡(x,t)||\mathbf{u}(x,t)| are obtained in (4.47a), upper and lower bounds bounds for σ⁡(x,t)\sigma(x,t) are given by (4.48), while upper bounds for |∇𝐮​(x,t)||\nabla\mathbf{u}(x,t)| and |∇σ​(x,t)||\nabla\sigma(x,t)| are established in (4.47b). We refer to Section 4.5 for these details.

1.3. Recent results concerning singularity formation for Euler

The literature concerning the formation and propagation of singularities for the compressible Euler equations (and related hyperbolic PDEs) is too vast to review here.77 7 In contrast, relatively few results have been established for the finite time singularity formation of the incompressible Euler equations; for instance, finite-time vorticity blowup remains open for the incompressible Euler equations posed on ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} or 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}, for Cc∞C_{c}^{\infty}, respectively C∞C^{\infty}, initial conditions. We note, however, that very recently, the finite time blowup for the vorticity was established in the presence of smooth solid boundaries [22, 23], for the equations posed in conical domains [35], or in the absence of boundaries for C1,αC^{1,\alpha} data with α\alpha very small [33, 21, 34, 36, 30]. In this section, we shall focus only on results for the Euler equations,88 8 There is a large literature concerning singularity formation for quasilinear wave equations; see the recent review articles [43, 68]. and review only those results for the multi-dimensional problem.99 9 For a detailed exposition of the 1D theory we refer the reader to [16, 31, 54] and references therein.

As noted above, it is well-known that the Euler equations develop finite-time gradient singularities from initial data which is as nice as it gets. The first proof of this fact was given in [67], using a proof by contradiction, inspired by the classical results [53, 49]. In recent decades, authors have given constructive proofs of singularity formation, which yield a very precise description of the solution at the time of the first gradient blowup. We categorize these constructive proofs into shock formation and smooth implosions.

1.3.1. Shock formation

Shock formation from smooth and localized initial conditions is, by now, well understood, up to the time of the first gradient singularity. In the context of irrotational solutions for the multi-dimensional Euler equations, blowup results based on ideas developed for second-order quasilinear wave equations and general relativity were established in [3, 2, 27, 29]; the latter two results were generalized to allow for vorticity and entropy in the Euler solution [55, 56]; results for 2D Euler solutions, with azimuthal symmetry, using modulated self-similar analysis were proven in [8, 7]; results for 3D Euler solutions in the absence of symmetry assumptions, based on modulated self-similar stability analysis were established in [9, 10]. In the context of shock development, results for Euler solutions with spherical symmetry were obtained in [72, 28], while results for Euler flows with azimuthal symmetry were proven in [6].

Very recently, shock formation past the time of the first singularity was analyzed in [66] and [1]. In [66] the last two authors of this paper analyze the evolution of fast-acoustic characteristic surfaces and use this smooth geometric information to describe the Euler solution up to a portion of the boundary of the maximal globally hyperbolic development (MGHD) of smooth Cauchy data, which includes both the singular set as well as the Cauchy horizon; the results of [1] evolve the Euler solution up to a portion of the boundary of the MGHD, containing only the singular set.

1.3.2. Smooth Implosions

The classical Guderley problem [42] deals with the implosion of a converging shock-wave, and the continuation as an expanding shock. In spite of the vast literature on this subject, the existence of a finite-time smooth implosion (without a shock already present in the solution at the initial time), was established only recently in [62, 63], and further refined in [11, 5]. While these results are inspired by the ansatz and general strategy in [42], the existence of C∞C^{\infty} self-similar implosion profiles requires a great deal of mathematical sophistication. Moreover, the stability of these solutions can only be established for finite-co-dimension perturbations which are not precisely quantified (see the numerical work [4] which attempts to quantify some of these instabilities). As explained in Section 2 below, this finite co-dimension stability of the smooth implosion profiles is one of the fundamental obstacles in proving vorticity blowup.

1.3.3. Solutions evolving from a singular state

While throughout this paper we are only concerned with smooth initial data, and we are only interested in the behavior of the resulting Euler solution up to the time of the first gradient singularity, there are many physically important problems in which the Euler evolution is initiated with data that already contains a singular state. A non-exhaustive list of examples includes the following: the short time evolution of discontinuous shock fronts [60, 59]; the shock reflection problem [14, 18]; the shock implosion [44] and shock explosion [45] problems; non-isentropic implosions with strictly positive pressure fields [46, 47]; the stability of rarefaction waves evolving from multi-dimensional Riemann data [57, 58]; the long-time stability of an irrotational expansion fan bounded by two shock surfaces [40]; and the ill-posedness of the Euler equations in multiple space dimensions for admissible weak solutions [26, 51, 32]. We also mention that there is a vast literature on transonic shocks for Euler both in the context of airfoils [64, 15] and in the setting of nozzles [71, 70, 69]; we refer the reader to the recent excellent review articles [65, 19, 17] for an extensive literature review.

1.3.4. Other singularities

A complete classification of all possible singularities that multi-dimensional and smooth Euler dynamics can reach in finite time is, to date, elusive. As discussed above, it is known that for regular initial data, at the time TT of the first singularity the Euler solution is capable of developing a shock, an implosion, and the goal of this paper is to show that it can also develop a vorticity blowup. It remains unsettled if these are the only possible first singularities attainable by smooth Euler evolution (with the classical ideal gas law equation of state). It is, for example, an open problem to determine whether vacuum1010 10 By this we mean that at the time TT of the first singularity, the density ρ⁡(⋅,T)\rho(\cdot,T) is equal to 00, at at least one spatial point. can form in finite time from smooth, localized, and non-vacuous initial data, in multiple space dimensions.1111 11 In one space dimension, vacuum cannot dynamically arise form from nice initial data without a shock forming first [12, 13].

2. Main ideas of the proof and comparison with previous results

Recall that in the two-dimensional setting of this paper, the specific vorticity ω/ρ\omega/\rho is transported, see (1.2). In order to prove Theorem 1.1, we construct initial data with non-trivial vorticity near R=0R=0, and for this data we construct an imploding solution by perturbing the radial implosion from [62]. We emphasize that the finitely many unstable modes of the self-similar blowup profile from [62] can potentially lead to either trivial vorticity, or to the destruction of the smooth implosion mechanism. To overcome this difficulty, we will crucially use the two-dimensional axisymmetric ansatz (1.4) and the structure of the equations (1.6), in order to establish full-stability of the swirl velocity, and hence of the vorticity.

2.4. Two key observations

First, in the linearized equations around the profile (U¯,0,Σ¯)(\bar{U},0,\bar{\Sigma}), the evolution of the perturbation 𝐀\mathbf{A} and those of the perturbation (𝐔~,Σ~)(\tilde{\mathbf{U}},\tilde{\Sigma}) are decoupled. That is, in (2.6) the linearized operators ℒU{\mathcal{L}}_{U} and ℒΣ{\mathcal{L}}_{\Sigma} do not depend on AA. Therefore, we can perform linear stability analysis of (𝐔~,Σ~)(\tilde{\mathbf{U}},\tilde{\Sigma}) and 𝐀\mathbf{A} separately. We will show that the linearized equations for (𝐔~,Σ~)(\tilde{\mathbf{U}},\tilde{\Sigma}) are stable upon modulating potentially finitely many unstable directions, developing a simpler stability proof. See Section 2.5.

Second, from (2.6b) we deduce that the linearized equation satisfied by A⁡(ξ,s)/ξA(\xi,s)/\xi is given by1515 15 Recall from (2.1c) that 𝐀⁡(y,s)=A⁡(ξ,s)​𝐞θ\mathbf{A}(y,s)=A(\xi,s)\mathbf{e}_{\theta}, and thus the self-similar vorticity at ξ=0\xi=0 is related to limξ→0+A⁡(ξ,s)/(2​ξ)\lim_{\xi\to 0^{+}}A(\xi,s)/(2\xi). We note that for a smooth perturbation, we have A⁡(0,s)=0A(0,s)=0 and hence A/ξA/\xi is well-defined.

∂t(Aξ)+(ξ+U¯)​∂ξ(Aξ)=−(r+2​U¯ξ)​(Aξ).\partial_{t}\Bigl(\frac{A}{\xi}\Bigr)+(\xi+\bar{U})\partial_{\xi}\Bigl(\frac{A}{\xi}\Bigr)=-\Bigl(r+2\frac{\bar{U}}{\xi}\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{A}{\xi}\Bigr).

Our crucial observation is that the blowup profile satisfies r+2​(U¯​(ξ)/ξ)<0r+2(\bar{U}(\xi)/\xi)<0 near ξ=0\xi=0, see (2.4e), which suggests the linear stability of A⁡(ξ)/ξA(\xi)/\xi near ξ=0\xi=0. Using this property, and the outgoing property of the self-similar velocity, namely that ξ+U¯​(ξ)≥κ​ξ\xi+\bar{U}(\xi)\geq\kappa\xi for for some κ>0\kappa>0 (see (2.4d)), we obtain that AA is stable in a suitably weighted space. These stability properties can also be captured by performing weighted L2L^{2} estimates with weights that are singular near ξ=0\xi=0. See Theorem 3.2.

In order to prove Theorem 1.1, we note that since the radial velocity 𝐔¯+𝐔~\bar{\mathbf{U}}+\tilde{\mathbf{U}} has 00 vorticity, and since 𝐀\mathbf{A} is stable, we can choose initial data for 𝐀\mathbf{A} in an open set (in the topology of a weighted Sobolev space) and thus construct non-trivial initial vorticity. Moreover, since (𝐔+𝐔~+𝐀)​(0,s)=0(\mathbf{U}+\tilde{\mathbf{U}}+\mathbf{A})(0,s)=0, the origin is a stationary point of the flow; thus, once we prove global nonlinear stability for (2.6)–(2.7), the finite-time blowup of vorticity claimed in (1.8d) now follows.

2.5. A new stability proof of implosion

The goal of this paper is to also develop a new stability proof of the implosion for the compressible Euler equations, which is simpler than the one given in [63, 61] (based on estimates of nonlinear wave equation), and in [5] (based on the transport structure of Riemann-type variables).

While in this paper we focus on the two-dimensional setting, the stability proof for the Euler equations in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with radially symmetric data (around a profile satisfying the properties in Lemma 2.2) would be the same, by setting 𝐀=0\mathbf{A}=0 in Sections 3, and 4. Our stability proof consists of the following steps.

Step 1: Weighted energy estimates

In the linear stability analysis of Section 3.2 we perform weighted H2​mH^{2m} estimates, with sufficiently large mm and a carefully designed weight φ2​m\varphi_{2m}, to obtain coercive estimates for the “top order” terms. The interior repulsive property (2.4b) allows us to obtain a damping term proportional to mm in the region |y|=ξ≤ξ1|y|=\xi\leq\xi_{1}, slightly beyond the sonic point ξs<ξ1\xi_{s}<\xi_{1}. For |y|=ξ>ξs|y|=\xi>\xi_{s}, we use the outgoing property related to the transport term (2.4c). We design a radially symmetric weight φ2​m​(y)\varphi_{2m}(y) decreasing in |y|=ξ|y|=\xi for ξ∈[ξ1,R2]\xi\in[\xi_{1},R_{2}], with R2R_{2} large enough. The monotonicity of the weight and the outgoing property provides a strong damping term in the energy estimates, as seen in Lemma 3.1. For |y|=ξ>R2|y|=\xi>R_{2}, due to the natural decay of the profile (2.4a), the linear dynamics is purely governed by the scaling terms, and is thus stable. The upshot of the linear stability analysis is that we obtain weighted H2​mH^{2m} estimates of the kind

(2.8) ⟨ℒ⁡(𝐔,Σ),(𝐔,Σ)⟩𝒳m≤−λ​‖(𝐔,Σ)‖𝒳m2+∫|y|≤R4ℛm​𝑑y,\langle{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbf{U},\Sigma),(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)\rangle_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\leq-\lambda\|(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}^{2}+\int_{|y|\leq R_{4}}{\mathcal{R}}_{m}dy,

for some inner product 𝒳m,m≥m0{\mathcal{X}}^{m},m\geq m_{0} with m0m_{0} sufficiently large, a suitably chosen R4>0R_{4}>0 and a coercive parameter λ>0\lambda>0 (uniform in m≥m0m\geq m_{0}). Here, ℛm{\mathcal{R}}_{m} denotes some “lower order” remainder terms (in terms of regularity, when compared to ‖(𝐔,Σ)‖𝒳m2\|(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}^{2}), which is made explicit in (3.13a). For the stability estimates of the 𝐀\mathbf{A} variable, we use the ideas discussed earlier in Section 2.4.

Step 2: Compact perturbation

To handle the lower order remainder term ℛm{\mathcal{R}}_{m} in (2.8), for each m≥m0m\geq m_{0}, in Section 3.3 we use Riesz representation to construct a linear operator 𝒦m{\mathcal{K}}_{m} from a bilinear form similar to

⟨𝒦m​f,g⟩𝒳m=∫χ​f⋅g​𝑑y,\langle{\mathcal{K}}_{m}f,g\rangle_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}=\int\chi f\cdot gdy,

where χ≥0\chi\geq 0 is a smooth cutoff function with χ=1\chi=1 for |y|≤R4|y|\leq R_{4}. The second term on the right side of (2.8) then arises as ⟨𝒦m​f,f⟩𝒳m\langle{\mathcal{K}}_{m}f,f\rangle_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}} for f=(𝐔,Σ)f=(\mathbf{U},\Sigma). Since the right hand side in the above display does not involve derivatives on ff and gg, and since χ\chi has a compact support, we can show that 𝒦m:𝒳m→𝒳m{\mathcal{K}}_{m}:{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m} is compact and that it has a smoothing effect 𝒦m:𝒳0→𝒳m+3{\mathcal{K}}_{m}:{\mathcal{X}}^{0}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m+3}. Afterwards, we obtain that ℒ−C¯​𝒦m{\mathcal{L}}-\bar{C}{\mathcal{K}}_{m} is dissipative, for C¯>0\bar{C}>0 chosen large enough.

Step 3: Construction of semigroup

To handle the compact perturbation, in Sections 3.4 and 3.5 we use semigroup theory to estimate the growth bound for the semigroups e(ℒ−𝒦m)​se^{({\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m})s} and eℒ​se^{{\mathcal{L}}s}. We prove a local well-posedness (LWP) result of the linearized equations in the space 𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m} in order to construct the semigroup. Note that the linearized equations are a symmetric hyperbolic system, whose LWP theory is classical.

Step 4: Smoothness of unstable direction

To construct a smooth initial data, in Section 3.6 we show that the potentially unstable directions of the linearized operators are spanned by smooth functions. An unstable direction ff satisfies a variant of the equation (ℒ−λ)​f=0({\mathcal{L}}-\lambda)f=0, for f∈𝒳m0f\in{\mathcal{X}}^{m_{0}}. Rewriting this as (ℒ−𝒦m−λ)​f=−𝒦m​f({\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m}-\lambda)f=-{\mathcal{K}}_{m}f, the smoothing effect of 𝒦m:𝒳0→𝒳m+3{\mathcal{K}}_{m}\colon{\mathcal{X}}^{0}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m+3}, the invertibility (ℒ−𝒦m−λ)−1:𝒳m→𝒳m({\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m}-\lambda)^{-1}\colon{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m}, and induction on m≥m0m\geq m_{0}, allows us to prove prove f∈C∞f\in C^{\infty}. See Lemma 3.9.

We note that Steps 2 & 4 discussed above resemble the functional approach to solve the elliptic equations, see e.g. [38]. The coercive estimates (2.8) allow us to construct the compact perturbation, which has a smoothing effect. These steps do not depend on specific structure of the equations.

Step 5: Nonlinear estimates

To close the nonlinear stability estimates, in Section 4 we decompose the perturbation 𝐕~=(𝐔~,𝐀,Σ~)\tilde{\mathbf{V}}=(\tilde{\mathbf{U}},\mathbf{A},\tilde{\Sigma}) into a stable part 𝐕~1\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1} and an unstable part 𝐕~2\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{2}, following the splitting method of [22]. For the unstable part, we represent 𝐕~2\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{2} using Duhamel’s formula and estimate it using the semigroup eℒ​se^{{\mathcal{L}}s}. The stable part 𝐕~1\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1} is estimated purely using energy estimates. Such a decomposition allows us to construct the global in self-similar time solution using a Banach fixed point argument and simpler bootstrap assumptions; moreover, this decomposition implicitly determines the stable initial data in the correct finite co-dimension space. See [48, 36] for related constructions of a global-in-time self-similar solution based on a Banach fixed point argument.

2.6. Comparison with the stability estimates in [63], [61] and [5]

Part of our stability estimates are similar to those in [63], [61], and in [5]: high order weighted Sobolev estimates to extract the dissipation, semigroup theory to estimate the compact perturbation, and finite co-dimension stability. Moreover, our H2​mH^{2m} stability estimates based on the variable (𝐔,Σ)(\mathbf{U},\Sigma) are inspired by [5] particularly in the region |y|=ξ≤ξs|y|=\xi\leq\xi_{s}. There are however several significant differences between our estimates and those in [63, 61, 5].

First, we do not localize the linearized operator, nor do we use Riemann-type variables to perform transport estimates. Instead, we exploit the outgoing properties of the flow (2.4c) by designing decreasing weights and incorporate such an effect in the weighted H2​mH^{2m} estimates. This allows us to obtain simpler nonlinear estimates. We note that weighted energy estimates with singular weights and weights depending on the profiles have been used successfully in a series of works by the first author and collaborators [24, 21, 25, 22, 20].

Second, we construct the semigroup based on the local well-posedness (LWP) of the linearized equations, which is obtained by appealing to a classical result. See Step 2 mentioned above, and Theorem 3.5. In contrast, in [5, 61], the construction is based on the notion of a maximal dissipative operator. Moreover, using the functional approach outlined in Step 4 above, we do not need to solve specific ODE or PDE problems as [5, 61], and hence we obtain simpler linear stability estimates.

Third, we use a Banach fixed point argument to obtain nonlinear finite co-dimension stability, different from the topological arguments employed in [5, 62].

Finally, we do not use the exterior repulsive property of the profile in the stability proof, which is required in [5], but may not hold for the similarity profile of 2D Euler equations (see the discussion in Remark 2.3). Thus, we cannot adopt the stability proof in [5] to establish the finite co-dimension stability of (𝐔~,Σ~)(\tilde{\mathbf{U}},\tilde{\Sigma}).

Our stability estimates can be extended to the compressible Navier-Stokes equations in the same settings as in [5, 63], with a minor modification since the diffusion is treated perturbatively, and the main term of the diffusion in the weighted estimates still has a good sign after performing integration by parts.

2.7. Comparison with the non-radial implosion in [11]

There appear to be essential difficulties in using the non-radial imploding solutions built in [11] to exhibit vorticity blowup for the compressible Euler equations in three space dimensions.

We recall that for d=3d=3, the specific vorticity of isentropic Euler satisfies the vector-transport equation

(2.9) ∂t(ωρ)+(𝐮⋅∇)(ωρ)=(𝐮⋅∇)(ωρ).\partial_{t}\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{\rho}\Bigr)+(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{\rho}\Bigr)=(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{\rho}\Bigr).

If we denote by X⁡(a,t)X(a,t) the Lagrangian flow1616 16 The Lagrangian flow XX solves the ODE ∂tX⁡(a,t)=u⁡(X⁡(t,a),t)\partial_{t}X(a,t)=u(X(t,a),t), with initial condition X⁡(a,0)=aX(a,0)=a. generated by uu, then (2.9) can be rewritten as

(2.10) (ωρ)​(X⁡(a,t),t)=∇aX​(a,t)​(ωρ)​(a,0).\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{\rho}\Bigr)(X(a,t),t)=\nabla_{a}X(a,t)\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{\rho}\Bigr)(a,0).

If we imagine 𝐮\mathbf{u} and σ\sigma (and hence ρ=(α​σ)1/α\rho=(\alpha\sigma)^{1/\alpha}) to be exactly the self-similar solutions to (1.3) built in [62] and [5], then the vorticity ω\omega would just be identically 00 by radial symmetry.

Nevertheless, we can replace the ω⁡(X⁡(a,t),t)\omega(X(a,t),t) appearing on the right side of (2.10) with a generic quantity

f=f⁡(X⁡(a,t),t)=ρ⁡(X⁡(a,t),t)​∇aX​(a,t)​f0ρ0​(a),f=f(X(a,t),t)=\rho(X(a,t),t)\nabla_{a}X(a,t)\tfrac{f_{0}}{\rho_{0}}(a),

and ask whether ‖f⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞\|f(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}} blows up as t↗Tt\scalebox{0.6}{$\nearrow$}T, with TT being the time of the implosion. In the next lemma we observe that ff remains uniformly bounded in aa and tt, as long as we choose the initial data f0f_{0} with a high-enough vanishing order at a=0a=0.

Lemma 2.4 (Not all transported quantities blow up in a 3D implosion).

Consider a self-similar profile (U¯,Σ¯)(\bar{U},\bar{\Sigma}) as constructed in [62] or [5], and let (𝐮,σ)(\mathbf{u},\sigma) be determined according to exact self-similarity from this profile via (2.1). Then, there exists k𝗏𝖺𝗇>0k_{\sf van}>0 such that for every smooth function f0f_{0} that satisfies |f0​(a)|≲min⁡(|a|k𝗏𝖺𝗇,1)|f_{0}(a)|\lesssim\min(|a|^{k_{\sf van}},1), we have

supa∈ℝ3,t∈[0,T)|ρ⁡(X⁡(a,t),t)​∇aX​(a,t)​f0ρ0​(a)|<+∞.\sup_{a\in\mathbb{R}^{3},t\in[0,T)}|\rho(X(a,t),t)\nabla_{a}X(a,t)\tfrac{f_{0}}{\rho_{0}}(a)|<+\infty.

The required vanishing order k𝗏𝖺𝗇k_{\sf van} is some constant that depends only on the profile (U¯,Σ¯)(\bar{U},\bar{\Sigma}), on rr, and on α\alpha.

We defer the proof to Appendix A. At this stage we note that the finite co-dimension of the initial data considered in [11] equals to the number of unstable directions of ℒ{\mathcal{L}}, which is a (sufficiently large) finite rank perturbation 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} to a maximally dissipative operator. Since the rank of 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} is used as a large parameter, the number of unstable directions k𝗎𝗇𝗌k_{\sf uns} is not quantified in [11], and therefore it is hard to determine whether k𝗎𝗇𝗌<k𝗏𝖺𝗇k_{\sf uns}<k_{\sf van}. Moreover, it is not shown in [11] that the finite co-dimension set of initial data contain any functions f0f_{0} violating the vanishing order f0=𝒪⁡(|a|k𝗏𝖺𝗇)f_{0}=\mathcal{O}(|a|^{k_{\sf van}}) near a=0a=0. Therefore, in light of Lemma 2.4 it is not clear whether the setting of [11] is at all amenable to vorticity blowup.

3.3. Compact perturbation via Riesz representation

In this section, using the estimates established earlier in Theorem 3.2, we construct a compact operator 𝒦m{\mathcal{K}}_{m} such that ℒ−𝒦m{\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m} is dissipative in 𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m}. For this purpose we fix m0≥6m_{0}\geq 6. We also recall from Lemma 3.3 that the Hilbert spaces {𝒳i}i≥0\{{\mathcal{X}}^{i}\}_{i\geq 0} are nested, with 𝒳i+1⊂𝒳i⊂…⊂𝒳0{\mathcal{X}}^{i+1}\subset{\mathcal{X}}^{i}\subset\ldots\subset{\mathcal{X}}^{0} for all i≥0i\geq 0; we will implicitly use this fact throughout this section.

Proposition 3.4.

For any m≥m0m\geq m_{0}, there exists a bounded linear operator 𝒦m:𝒳0→𝒳m{\mathcal{K}}_{m}\colon{\mathcal{X}}^{0}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m} with:

  • (a)

    for any f∈𝒳0f\in{\mathcal{X}}^{0} we have

    supp⁡(𝒦m​f)⊂B⁡(0,4​R4),{\rm supp}({\mathcal{K}}_{m}f)\subset B(0,4R_{4}),

    where R4R_{4} is chosen in Theorem 3.2 (in particular, it is independent of mm);

  • (b)

    the operator 𝒦m{\mathcal{K}}_{m} is compact from 𝒳m→𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m};

  • (c)

    the enhanced smoothing property 𝒦m:𝒳0→𝒳m+3{\mathcal{K}}_{m}:{\mathcal{X}}^{0}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m+3} holds;

  • (d)

    the operator ℒ−𝒦m{\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m} is dissipative on 𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m} and we have the estimate

    (3.30) ⟨(ℒ−𝒦m)​f,f⟩𝒳m≤−λ​‖f‖𝒳m2\langle({\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m})f,f\rangle_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\leq-\lambda\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}^{2}

    for all f∈{(𝐔,Σ)∈𝒳m:ℒ⁡(𝐔,Σ)∈𝒳m}f\in\{(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)\in{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\colon{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)\in{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\}, ℒ=(ℒU,ℒS){\mathcal{L}}=({\mathcal{L}}_{U},{\mathcal{L}}_{S}), and where λ>0\lambda>0 is the parameter from (3.13a) (in particular, it is independent of mm).

Item (d) shows that ℒ{\mathcal{L}} is a compact perturbation of the dissipative operator 𝒟m≜ℒ−𝒦m{\mathcal{D}}_{m}\triangleq{\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m} in 𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m}, for any m≥m0m\geq m_{0}. By further regularizing 𝒦m{\mathcal{K}}_{m} one could define 𝒦m:𝒳0→𝒳∞=∩m≥0𝒳m{\mathcal{K}}_{m}:{\mathcal{X}}^{0}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{\infty}=\cap_{m\geq 0}{\mathcal{X}}^{m}, but we do not need this extra regularity and thus do not seek this refinement; we only need the 𝒳m+3{\mathcal{X}}^{m+3}-regularity claimed in item (c) in order to simplify the nonlinear estimates in Section 4.4.2.

Proof.

Fix R4R_{4} as in Theorem 3.2. We let 0≤χ1,χ2≤10\leq\chi_{1},\chi_{2}\leq 1 be smooth cutoff functions such that

(3.31a) χ1​(y)=1,|y|≤2​R4,χ1​(y)=0,|y|≥4​R4,\displaystyle\chi_{1}(y)=1,\ |y|\leq 2R_{4},\quad\chi_{1}(y)=0,\ |y|\geq 4R_{4},
(3.31b) χ2​(y)=1,|y|≤4​R4,χ2​(y)=0,|y|>8​R4.\displaystyle\chi_{2}(y)=1,\ |y|\leq 4R_{4},\quad\chi_{2}(y)=0,\ |y|>8R_{4}.

Riesz representation

We consider the bilinear form Bm​(⋅,⋅):𝒳0×𝒳m→ℝB_{m}(\cdot,\cdot)\colon{\mathcal{X}}^{0}\times{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\to{\mathbb{R}} defined by

3.4. Construction of the semigroup

For any m≥m0m\geq m_{0} we construct the strongly continuous semigroups

eℒ​s:𝒳m→𝒳m,e𝒟m​s:𝒳m→𝒳m,ℒ=(ℒU,ℒΣ)=𝒟m+𝒦m.e^{{\mathcal{L}}s}:{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m},\quad e^{{\mathcal{D}}_{m}s}:{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\to{\mathcal{X}}^{m},\quad{\mathcal{L}}=({\mathcal{L}}_{U},{\mathcal{L}}_{\Sigma})={\mathcal{D}}_{m}+{\mathcal{K}}_{m}.

by directly solving the associated linear PDEs. Here 𝒦m{\mathcal{K}}_{m} is as constructed in Proposition 3.4. In this section, without loss of generality we consider semigroups defined for s≥0s\geq 0, although in applications for Section 4 the interval s≥s𝗂𝗇s\geq s_{\mathsf{in}} is the relevant one.

3.4.1. From linear PDEs to semigroups

The relation between linear evolutionary PDEs and semigroups is classical; see e.g. [37]. Following Definition 6.1, Chapter II of [37], we consider the abstract initial value problem for a linear operator 𝒜:D⁡(𝒜)⊂X→X{\mathcal{A}}:D({\mathcal{A}})\subset X\to X with domain D⁡(𝒜)D({\mathcal{A}}):

(3.35) dd​t​u​(t)=𝒜​u​(t),t≥0,u⁡(0)=x∈X,\tfrac{d}{dt}u(t)={\mathcal{A}}u(t),\quad t\geq 0,\quad u(0)=x\in X,

where XX is a Banach space. A function u:ℝ+→Xu:{\mathbb{R}}_{+}\to X is a (classical) solution of (3.35) if uu is continuously differentiable with respect to XX, u⁡(t)∈D⁡(𝒜)u(t)\in D({\mathcal{A}}) for all t≥0t\geq 0, and (3.35) holds in XX for all t>0t>0. We use the notation u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) to denote a solution uu from initial data x∈Xx\in X, at time tt. We recall:

Theorem 3.5 (Theorem 6.7, Chapter II, [37]).

Let 𝒜:D⁡(𝒜)⊂X→X{\mathcal{A}}:D({\mathcal{A}})\subset X\to X be a closed operator. The following properties are equivalent:

  • (a)

    𝒜{\mathcal{A}} generates a strongly continuous semigroup.

  • (b)

    For every x∈D⁡(𝒜)x\in D({\mathcal{A}}), there exists a unique solution u⁡(x,⋅)u(x,\cdot) of the initial value problem (3.35). The operator 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} has dense domain, and for every sequence {xn}n≥1⊂D⁡(𝒜)\{x_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}\subset D({\mathcal{A}}) satisfying limn→∞xn=0\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}=0, one has limn→∞u⁡(xn,t)=0\lim_{n\to\infty}u(x_{n},t)=0 uniformly on compact intervals [0,t0][0,t_{0}].

The above theorem states that 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} generates a strongly continuous semi-group if and only if the linear PDEs is well-posed: (3.35) has a unique solution, and satisfies continuous dependence on the data.

3.4.2. Solving linear PDEs

We define the domains of the operators ℒ=(ℒU,ℒΣ){\mathcal{L}}=({\mathcal{L}}_{U},{\mathcal{L}}_{\Sigma}) and 𝒟m=ℒ−𝒦m{\mathcal{D}}_{m}={\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m} as

(3.36) D⁡(𝒟m)=D⁡(ℒ)≜{(𝐔,Σ)∈𝒳m,ℒ⁡(𝐔,Σ)∈𝒳m}.D({\mathcal{D}}_{m})=D({\mathcal{L}})\triangleq\{(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)\in{\mathcal{X}}^{m},{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)\in{\mathcal{X}}^{m}\}.

Recall from (2.6d) and (2.6f) that the linearized operator ℒ=(ℒU,ℒΣ){\mathcal{L}}=({\mathcal{L}}_{U},{\mathcal{L}}_{\Sigma}) is defined via

(3.37a) ℒU​(𝐔,Σ)\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{U}(\mathbf{U},\Sigma) =−(r−1)𝐔−(y+𝐔¯)⋅∇𝐔−𝐔⋅∇𝐔¯−αΣ∇Σ¯−αΣ¯∇Σ,\displaystyle=-(r-1)\mathbf{U}-(y+\bar{\mathbf{U}})\cdot\nabla\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{U}\cdot\nabla\bar{\mathbf{U}}-\alpha\Sigma\nabla\bar{\Sigma}-\alpha\bar{\Sigma}\nabla\Sigma,
(3.37b) ℒΣ​(𝐔,Σ)\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{\Sigma}(\mathbf{U},\Sigma) =−(r−1)​Σ−(y+𝐔¯)⋅∇Σ−𝐔⋅∇Σ¯−α​div⁡(𝐔¯)​Σ−α​div⁡(𝐔)​Σ¯,\displaystyle=-(r-1)\Sigma-(y+\bar{\mathbf{U}})\cdot\nabla\Sigma-\mathbf{U}\cdot\nabla\bar{\Sigma}-\alpha\operatorname{div}(\bar{\mathbf{U}})\Sigma-\alpha\operatorname{div}(\mathbf{U})\bar{\Sigma},
resulting in the linearized versions of the evolution equations (2.6a) and (2.6c)

Note that ℒ{\mathcal{L}} does not involve AA, so that (3.37) is a closed evolution for (𝐔,Σ)(\mathbf{U},\Sigma), which is why we drop the dependence on AA. Denote 𝐕=(𝐔,Σ)=(U1,U2,Σ)⊂ℝ3\mathbf{V}=(\mathbf{U},\Sigma)=(U_{1},U_{2},\Sigma)\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. The linearized equations (3.37c) may be written in the form of a symmetric hyperbolic system

4. Nonlinear stability

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.1, by constructing global solutions (𝐔,Σ,𝐀)(\mathbf{U},\Sigma,\mathbf{A}) to (2.3), with a number of desirable properties, in the vicinity of the stationary profile (𝐔¯,Σ¯,0)(\bar{\mathbf{U}},\bar{\Sigma},0). Throughout this section we fix m≥m0m\geq m_{0}, where m0m_{0} is sufficiently large, as in Theorem 3.2.

4.1. Decomposition of the solution

We will use 𝐕=(𝐔,Σ,𝐀)\mathbf{V}=(\mathbf{U},\Sigma,\mathbf{A}) to denote the nonlinear solution to (2.3). As in (2.5), we denote the perturbation to the stationary profile as

In (4.2), and in the remainder of the section, we have abused notation two-fold. First, in (4.2a) we note that the output of the 𝒦m{\mathcal{K}}_{m} operator is an element of 𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m} (hence, a 𝐔\mathbf{U} and a Σ\Sigma) and so it does not contain an 𝐀\mathbf{A}-component (as is required by the 𝐕~1\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1} representation in (4.1)); as such, in (4.2a) we write 𝒦m​(𝐕~1)=𝒦m​(𝐔~1,Σ~1){\mathcal{K}}_{m}(\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1})={\mathcal{K}}_{m}(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1},\tilde{\Sigma}_{1}) to mean (𝒦m​(𝐔~1,Σ~1),0)({\mathcal{K}}_{m}(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1},\tilde{\Sigma}_{1}),0), i.e., 𝒦m​(𝐕~1){\mathcal{K}}_{m}(\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1}) does not act on the 𝐀\mathbf{A}-component. There are a few important advantages to the decomposition2424 24 This decomposition was first developed in [22] for stable blowup analysis of the 3D incompressible Euler equations. (4.1) and the definitions (4.2). First, the part 𝐕~2\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{2}, which is used to capture unstable parts, is decoupled from the equation of 𝐕~1\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1} at the linear level, and so we can obtain decay estimates for 𝐕~1\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1} directly using energy estimates and the dissipativity of (ℒ−𝒦m,ℒA)({\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{K}}_{m},{\mathcal{L}}_{A}) (see (3.13b) and (3.30)), without appealing to semigroups. Second, we can obtain a representation formula (and an estimate) for 𝐕~2\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{2} by using Duhamel’s formula

for some initial data 𝐕2,i​n\mathbf{V}_{2,in}, to be chosen later. We obtain bounds for the full nonlinear system (4.2) by treating the nonlinear terms perturbatively.

The Duhamel representation (4.3) for the unstable part of the perturbation is deceivingly simple; this is because we did not yet specify the initial data 𝐕~2,i​n\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{2,in}. The goal of this appendix is to gather a few functional analytic bounds that are used throughout the paper. First, we record a Leibniz rule for radially symmetric vectors/scalars.

|Δm(fdiv(𝐆)−fdiv(Δm𝐆)−2m∇f⋅Δm𝐆|\displaystyle|\Delta^{m}(f\operatorname{div}(\mathbf{G})-f\operatorname{div}(\Delta^{m}\mathbf{G})-2m\nabla f\cdot\Delta^{m}\mathbf{G}| ≲∑1≤j≤2​mm⁡|∇2​m+1−jf|⋅|∇j𝐆|,\displaystyle\lesssim_{m}\sum_{1\leq j\leq 2m}|\nabla^{2m+1-j}f|\cdot|\nabla^{j}\mathbf{G}|,

Lastly, we record the following product estimates for the functional spaces 𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m} defined in (3.14). It is convenient to state estimates for a general dimension dd, not just for d=2d=2. For this purpose, we recall from (3.15) that φg=⟨y⟩−κ1−d\varphi_{g}=\langle y\rangle^{-\kappa_{1}-d}, with κ1=1/4∈(0,1)\kappa_{1}=1/4\in(0,1). Moreover, we recall from Lemma 3.1 that the weights φm\varphi_{m} satisfy φm(y)≍m⟨y⟩m\varphi_{m}(y)\asymp_{m}\langle y\rangle^{m}, and |∇φm(y)|≲mφm−1(y)|\nabla\varphi_{m}(y)|\lesssim_{m}\varphi_{m-1}(y).

Lemma C.4.

Let m≥d/2m\geq d/2. For f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} which lies in 𝒳m{\mathcal{X}}^{m} and 0≤i≤2​m−d0\leq i\leq 2m-d, we have

(C.5) |∇if(y)|≲m∥f∥𝒳m⟨y⟩−i+κ12,|\nabla^{i}f(y)|\lesssim_{m}\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\langle y\rangle^{-i+\frac{\kappa_{1}}{2}},

pointwise for y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Moreover, for any i≤2​mi\leq 2m, j≤2​nj\leq 2n, with i≤2​m−di\leq 2m-d or j≤2​n−dj\leq 2n-d, and for any β≥κ1/2\beta\geq\kappa_{1}/2, we have

(C.6) ∥∇if∇jg⟨y⟩i+j−βφg1/2∥L2≲m,n,β∥f∥𝒳m∥g∥𝒳n.\|\nabla^{i}f\;\nabla^{j}g\;\langle y\rangle^{i+j-\beta}\varphi_{g}^{1/2}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim_{m,n,\beta}\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\|g\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{n}}.
Proof.

Fix 1≤i≤2​m−d1\leq i\leq 2m-d. By a standard density argument we can assume that ∇if∈Cc∞​(ℝd)\nabla^{i}f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Consider the cone with vertex at yy extending towards infinity: Ω(y)≜{z∈ℝd:zjsgn(yj)≥|yj|,∀1≤j≤d}\Omega(y)\triangleq\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\colon z_{j}\mathrm{sgn}(y_{j})\geq|y_{j}|,\forall 1\leq j\leq d\}. In particular, for any z∈Ω⁡(y)z\in\Omega(y) have |z|≥|y||z|\geq|y|. By integrating on rays extending to infinity, we have

|∇if(y)|≲∫Ω⁡(y)|∂1∂2..∂d∇if(z)|dz.|\nabla^{i}f(y)|\lesssim\int_{\Omega(y)}|\partial_{1}\partial_{2}..\partial_{d}\nabla^{i}f(z)|dz.

Upon letting δ2=−(κ1+d)\delta_{2}=-(\kappa_{1}+d) and δ1=1\delta_{1}=1 (choices with are consistent with the weights in (3.14)), from Cauchy-Schwartz, Lemma C.2 with βn=2​n+δ2\beta_{n}=2n+\delta_{2} (applicable since i+d≤2​mi+d\leq 2m), and Lemma C.3 with φ~n=φn​φg1/2≍⟨y⟩n​φg1/2\tilde{\varphi}_{n}=\varphi_{n}\varphi_{g}^{1/2}\asymp\langle y\rangle^{n}\varphi_{g}^{1/2}, we deduce

|∇if​(y)|\displaystyle|\nabla^{i}f(y)| ≲‖⟨z⟩i+d+δ22​∇i+df​(z)‖L2​(Ω​(y))​(∫|z|≥|y|⟨z⟩−2​i−2​d−δ2​𝑑z)1/2\displaystyle\lesssim\|\langle z\rangle^{i+d+\frac{\delta_{2}}{2}}\nabla^{i+d}f(z)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega(y))}\Big(\int_{|z|\geq|y|}\langle z\rangle^{-2i-2d-\delta_{2}}dz\Big)^{1/2}
≲‖⟨z⟩12​βi+d​∇i+df​(z)‖L2​(ℝd)​(∫|y|∞⟨R⟩−2​i−2​d+(κ1+d)​Rd−1​𝑑R)1/2\displaystyle\lesssim\|\langle z\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}\beta_{i+d}}\nabla^{i+d}f(z)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\Big(\int_{|y|}^{\infty}\langle R\rangle^{-2i-2d+(\kappa_{1}+d)}R^{d-1}dR\Big)^{1/2}
≲(‖⟨z⟩12​β2​m​∇2​mf​(z)‖L2​(ℝd)+‖⟨z⟩12​β0​f​(z)‖L2​(ℝd))​(∫|y|∞⟨R⟩−2​i+κ1−1​d​⟨R⟩)1/2\displaystyle\lesssim\left(\|\langle z\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}\beta_{2m}}\nabla^{2m}f(z)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}+\|\langle z\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}\beta_{0}}f(z)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\right)\Big(\int_{|y|}^{\infty}\langle R\rangle^{-2i+\kappa_{1}-1}d\langle R\rangle\Big)^{1/2}
≲‖f‖𝒳m​⟨y⟩−i+κ12.\displaystyle\lesssim\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\langle y\rangle^{-i+\frac{\kappa_{1}}{2}}.

For the last inequality we have crucially used that 2​i−κ1>02i-\kappa_{1}>0, which holds since i≥1i\geq 1.

For i=0i=0, the aforementioned inequality (namely, 2​i−κ1>02i-\kappa_{1}>0) does not hold, and so the integral appearing in the above estimates does not converge. Instead, using the fundamental theorem of calculus and the decay estimate for |∇f||\nabla f| obtained above, we have

|f⁡(y)|≤|f⁡(0)|+∫0|y||∇f|​(t​y|y|)​𝑑t≲|f⁡(0)|+‖f‖𝒳m​∫0|y|⟨t⟩−1+κ12​𝑑t≲|f⁡(0)|+‖f‖𝒳m​⟨y⟩κ12.|f(y)|\leq|f(0)|+\int_{0}^{|y|}|\nabla f|\Big(\frac{ty}{|y|}\Big)dt\lesssim|f(0)|+\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\int_{0}^{|y|}\langle t\rangle^{-1+\frac{\kappa_{1}}{2}}dt\lesssim|f(0)|+\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\langle y\rangle^{\frac{\kappa_{1}}{2}}.

To conclude the proof of (C.5) for i=0i=0, we note that |f⁡(0)|≲‖f‖𝒳m|f(0)|\lesssim\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}. To see this, let χ\chi be a smooth bump function 0≤χ≤10\leq\chi\leq 1 with χ≡1\chi\equiv 1 for |y|≤1/2|y|\leq 1/2 and χ≡0\chi\equiv 0 for |y|≥1|y|\geq 1. Then, we have |f⁡(0)|≤‖χ​f‖L∞≲‖χ​f‖H2​m≲‖χ​f‖𝒳m≲‖f‖𝒳m|f(0)|\leq\|\chi f\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|\chi f\|_{H^{2m}}\lesssim\|\chi f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\lesssim\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}, where the last inequality holds by Lemma C.2 and Lemma C.3.

In order to prove (C.6), assume without loss of generality that i≤2​m−di\leq 2m-d. Using (C.5), and recalling that φg=⟨y⟩−κ1−d\varphi_{g}=\langle y\rangle^{-\kappa_{1}-d}, we have

∥∇if∇jg⟨y⟩i+j−βφg1/2∥L2≲m∥⟨y⟩i−κ12∇if∥L∞∥∇jg⟨y⟩j−β+κ12φg1/2∥L2≲m∥f∥𝒳m∥∇jg⟨y⟩j−β−d2∥L2.\|\nabla^{i}f\nabla^{j}g\langle y\rangle^{i+j-\beta}\varphi_{g}^{1/2}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim_{m}\|\langle y\rangle^{i-\frac{\kappa_{1}}{2}}\nabla^{i}f\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\nabla^{j}g\langle y\rangle^{j-\beta+\frac{\kappa_{1}}{2}}\varphi_{g}^{1/2}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim_{m}\|f\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}}\|\nabla^{j}g\langle y\rangle^{j-\beta-\frac{d}{2}}\|_{L^{2}}.

Next, Lemma C.2 with δ1=1\delta_{1}=1 and δ2=−(κ1+d)\delta_{2}=-(\kappa_{1}+d), to obtain

∥∇jg⟨y⟩j−β−d2∥L2≲∥∇jg⟨y⟩j+δ22∥L2≲m∥g∥𝒳m,\|\nabla^{j}g\langle y\rangle^{j-\beta-\frac{d}{2}}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|\nabla^{j}g\langle y\rangle^{j+\frac{\delta_{2}}{2}}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim_{m}\|g\|_{{\mathcal{X}}^{m}},

where we have used that −β−d/2≤δ2/2-\beta-d/2\leq\delta_{2}/2, which holds since β≥κ1/2\beta\geq\kappa_{1}/2. MM □\square
